query: W melts near 3422 °C, whereas Cu boils near 2562 °C, so conventional induction or arc-plasma casting cannot readily yield a uniform W–Cu material. Phase separation and void formation can impair thermal transport. Filling a W skeleton with molten Cu or Cu powder can leave defects; spark-plasma sintering and mechanical alloying can produce finer, more uniform structures but can also leave voids; vapor-coated W powders have been sintered to achieve near-perfect contact between the constituents; and metal 3D printing has also been explored. Starting from W particles or connected W regions within a Cu matrix for heat transfer under irradiation in fusion-reactor joints, what single intervention could overcome these limitations while preserving mechanical durability? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts an outcome relative to a named existing fabrication baseline, defines the processing and service boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment and observations that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Pre-coating tungsten particles with a thin, conformal nickel layer will improve copper wettability during consolidation, reducing phase‐separation-induced voids and defects while maintaining mechanical durability in W–Cu composites for fusion-reactor heat transfer joints.
generation.material_initial_state: A composite precursor consisting of tungsten particles or connected tungsten regions embedded within a copper matrix (uncoated W particles as conventionally produced).
generation.intervention: Apply a nanoscale nickel coating to the tungsten surfaces using physical vapor deposition (or an equivalent surface‐engineering method) prior to consolidation/sintering with copper.
generation.conditions: The coating and subsequent consolidation are carried out under processing temperatures below the boiling point of copper, and the composite is intended for service under high-temperature (≈1000 K and above) irradiation conditions encountered in fusion-reactor joints.
generation.structural_mediator: The interfacial Ni layer acting as a wetting enhancer at the W–Cu boundary.
generation.mechanism: Nickel reduces the interfacial energy between tungsten and molten copper, thereby improving copper infiltration and bonding during consolidation. This enhanced wetting suppresses void nucleation and phase separation, leading to a more uniform microstructure that preserves thermal transport and mechanical durability under irradiation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline produced by standard methods (such as spark-plasma sintering or mechanical alloying of uncoated W particles), the Ni-coated system is predicted to exhibit a lower void fraction and more continuous W–Cu interfaces, resulting in improved thermal conductivity and mechanical performance during service.
generation.baseline: Conventional processing routes that rely on direct consolidation (e.g., spark-plasma sintering, mechanical alloying, or vapor-coating without interfacial wetting tailoring) of uncoated tungsten particles in a copper matrix.
generation.boundary: This intervention is specifically intended for processing below Cu’s boiling temperature and for use in fusion-reactor joint regions where the composite is exposed to high heat flux and irradiation. Its effectiveness outside these temperature and irradiation regimes is not addressed.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal nickel coating thickness and processing parameters (e.g., deposition conditions, sintering temperature and pressure) require further optimization. Additionally, potential Ni diffusion or intermetallic formation under prolonged irradiation remains to be evaluated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of W–Cu composite samples: one set with tungsten particles pre-coated with a thin Ni layer and one set with standard uncoated tungsten particles. Process both sets using identical consolidation conditions (e.g., spark-plasma sintering) under temperatures below the copper boiling point. Following consolidation, subject both sample sets to thermal cycling and simulated fusion-relevant irradiation.
measurements: Void fraction and microstructural uniformity via high-resolution tomography and electron microscopy.
Thermal conductivity measurements across the joint region.
Mechanical durability tests (e.g., compressive strength, fracture toughness) before and after thermal/irradiation cycling.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ni-coated samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in void fraction and an improvement in thermal and mechanical performance relative to the uncoated control samples under identical processing and test conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Key components in magnetic fusion reactors, such as the divertor or the plasma-facing materials (PFMs), are required to have stringent properties including low activation, high melting point, good thermomechanical properties, low sputter erosion, and low tritium retention/codeposition. They must operate at high temperature (≥1000 K) for long durations (>10 7 s), without failure or extensive erosion while exposed to large plasma heat and an intense mixture of ionized and energetic neutral species of hydrogen isotopes (D and T), He ash (fluxes, >10 24 m −2 s −1 ), and neutrons ( [1] ). Tungsten (W) is the leading PFM candidate because of its high melting temperature, low erosion rates, and small tritium retention. These advantages are unfortunately coupled with very low fracture toughness characterized by brittle transgranular and intergranular failure regimes, which severely restrict the useful operating temperature window and also create a range of fabrication difficulties. Furthermore, blistering at moderate temperature (<800 K) by D and He ( [2] , [3] ) and the formation of pits, holes, and bubbles by He at higher temperature (>1600 K) ( [4] ) have all been observed.
